questions.stem: According to the wounded Captain, what did Macbeth do to the rebel Macdonwald?
options: Captured him and sent him to Duncan for trial
Drove him back by sea to the Western Isles
Split him open and set his head on the battlements
Wounded him and let him flee to the Norwegian camp
questions.why: The Captain reports that Macbeth cut Macdonwald open "from the nave to the chops" and fixed his head on the battlements; the rebel was neither captured nor allowed to escape.

questions.stem: Speaking of the executed Thane of Cawdor, Duncan says, "There's no art to find the mind's construction in the face." Why is this line ironic as Macbeth enters right after it?
options: Duncan is about to trust another man whose looks hide treacherous thoughts
Duncan has already guessed that Macbeth wants the crown
Cawdor actually died without confessing any of his crimes
Macbeth has come to plead for Cawdor's life and title
questions.why: Duncan admits he was fooled by Cawdor and at once heaps trust on Macbeth, who in the same scene hides his "black and deep desires"; Malcolm reports that Cawdor did confess, so C is false.

questions.stem: Soon after Nick moves to West Egg, what makes him stop feeling lonely?
options: His Finnish housekeeper starts cooking his evening meals
A newcomer stops him on the road to ask the way to West Egg village
A young man from his office moves into the bungalow with him
Daisy telephones to invite him to dinner in East Egg
questions.why: Being asked for directions makes Nick feel like a settler; the coworker who found the house was sent to Washington, so Nick moved in alone.

questions.stem: Daisy repeats what she said after her daughter was born: "I hope she’ll be a fool—that’s the best thing a girl can be in this world, a beautiful little fool." What does the line suggest about Daisy's view of her world?
options: A girl will suffer less if she does not see too clearly how things are
She wishes her child had been born a boy instead
She is joking that her daughter already looks like Tom
She wants her daughter to grow up as sophisticated as herself
questions.why: Speaking from her own sense of abandonment, Daisy implies that knowing less would hurt less; she says she is glad it is a girl, so B is wrong.

questions.stem: According to Walton's first letter, what kept him from going to sea as a boy?
options: His sister Margaret's fear that he would drown on a voyage
His father's dying wish, which forbade his uncle to let him go
His uncle Thomas's own refusal to let him leave school
A weak constitution that left him unfit for hard labor
questions.why: B: the father's dying injunction bound the uncle; uncle Thomas only supplied the books of voyages, so C reverses who forbade it.

questions.stem: When Walton says he would sacrifice everything to his enterprise, the stranger cries, "Do you share my madness? Have you drank also of the intoxicating draught?" What does the image of the draught suggest?
options: Walton has been drinking with the crew to keep up his spirits
Walton's thirst for discovery is a dangerous craving the stranger once gave in to
The stranger blames the brandy the sailors forced him to swallow
The stranger envies Walton's hope and wishes to share it
questions.why: B: the 'draught' is Walton's ambition, which the stranger calls a shared 'madness' and urges him to 'dash the cup' away; the brandy in C is a literal detail, not the meaning.

questions.stem: When Edna comes back from the beach, what does Mr. Pontellier take from his vest pocket and hand to her?
options: The rings she had left with him before bathing
A ten-dollar bill to spend on the children's treats
A letter from her sister who is away in the East
The key to the family's bath-house on the beach
questions.why: Edna silently reaches out and he returns her rings; the ten-dollar bill stays in his pocket for the game at Klein's.

questions.stem: After the ladies praise the box of treats from New Orleans, the narrator adds: "Mrs. Pontellier was forced to admit that she knew of none better." What does the word "forced" suggest?
options: Her husband ordered her to praise him.
She is jealous that the other ladies admire her husband.
She is embarrassed that the box is smaller than usual.
She agrees under pressure, without real warmth.
questions.why: Coming right after the scene of the night before, "forced" shows Edna conceding the point because the facts and the company require it, not out of feeling.

questions.stem: In Scene 1, the Ghost returns and Horatio begs it to speak. What happens just as it seems about to answer?
options: Barnardo cries out and frightens it away
The bell strikes one and it falls silent
A cock crows and it starts away
Hamlet arrives and it turns toward him
questions.why: Barnardo says the Ghost "was about to speak, when the cock crew," and Horatio describes it starting "like a guilty thing"; Hamlet is not on the platform in Scene 1.

questions.stem: When Claudius turns to "my cousin Hamlet, and my son," Hamlet says aside, "A little more than kin, and less than kind." What does the aside suggest?
options: He is grateful that Claudius has named him the next heir
He thinks Claudius has no royal blood at all
He would rather be called a son than a cousin
He is doubly related to Claudius yet feels no warmth
questions.why: As uncle and now stepfather, Claudius is "more than kin," yet Hamlet feels nothing "kind" (natural or loving) toward him; the bitter aside rules out gratitude.

questions.stem: According to the narrator, what was the "chief tragic event" in the life of the old Inspector?
options: The loss of his savings in a failed trading voyage
A goose so tough it took an axe and handsaw to divide
Losing his place when the Whigs came into power
A shipwreck he barely survived as a young sailor
questions.why: The narrator jokes that a goose so tough it needed an axe and handsaw was the old man's great tragedy; the deaths of his three wives and most of his children cost him only "one brief sigh," which is the point of the satire.

questions.stem: Placing the faded cloth on his chest, the narrator feels "as if the letter were not of red cloth, but red-hot iron." What does this sensation suggest?
options: The old cloth had been treated with a dye that stung the skin
He suspects the letter is a fake made by some later clerk
The old symbol still holds a painful, almost bodily power
He is excited by how much money the relic might bring him
questions.why: The letter seems to burn like a brand, so its meaning reaches his feelings before his mind can explain it; he shudders and drops it, which fits none of the practical readings.

questions.stem: In Chapter 1, Lockwood confesses what happened at the seaside last summer when a young woman he admired finally returned his look. What did he do?
options: He proposed to her, but her mother refused to allow the match
He grew cold until she thought she had been mistaken
He wrote her a poem and left the coast before she could reply
He followed her home and was turned away at the door
questions.why: Lockwood admits he "shrunk icily" into himself until the young woman doubted her own senses and left with her mother; he never declared himself, so there was no proposal or poem.

questions.stem: Lockwood notices "a range of gaunt thorns all stretching their limbs one way, as if craving alms of the sun." What does this image suggest about the setting?
options: Wind-bent, they look like beggars pleading for warmth
The trees are carefully trained by Heathcliff's servants
The house faces south and enjoys unusual sunshine
The thorns are dying because no one has watered them
questions.why: The "gaunt" thorns are bent by the north wind and personified as beggars asking the sun for charity, an image of a harsh, starved, exposed place; nobody tends this garden.

questions.stem: After John Reed makes Jane fetch the book she was reading behind the curtain, what does he do with it?
options: Tears out the pictures and drops them in the fire
Hurls it at her, so that she falls and cuts her head
Hides it and tells his mother that Jane stole it
Hands it to Eliza and orders Jane out of the breakfast-room
questions.why: John throws the volume at Jane; she falls against the door and cuts her head, which is why blood trickles down her neck during the fight. He claims the books are his but does not hide or destroy this one.

questions.stem: Among Bewick's pictures, Jane lingers over "the rock standing up alone in a sea of billow and spray" and a wreck under a cold moon. Why are such images fitting for her that afternoon?
options: They show her plan to run away to sea when she is older
They echo her own isolation and the storm outside the window
They are the only pictures the Reeds allow her to look at
They remind her of a seaside holiday she spent with the Reeds
questions.why: Shut out from the family group and gazing at a rain-lashed lawn, Jane is drawn to images of lone rocks and wrecks that mirror her own state; nothing suggests a plan to go to sea or a rule about which pictures she may see.
